Bear case: Halozyme's single biggest vulnerability is not patent expiration in the abstract — it is that its switching-cost moat has already been breached by a competing platform for one of the largest franchises in pharma. Alteogen's ALT-B4 hyaluronidase is a direct rival to ENHANZE, and Merck selected Alteogen's technology (not Halozyme's ENHANZE) for the subcutaneous formulation of Keytruda — the world's best-selling drug and exactly the kind of marquee franchise the ENHANZE thesis assumes is locked in once approved. That is proof the 'once approved, switching is a multi-year multi-hundred-million-dollar undertaking' argument does not hold for new formulation decisions, only for formulations already filed on ENHANZE — meaning every future deal Halozyme has NOT yet signed (unlike the fresh Incyte win) is genuinely contestable, not a bolt-on annuity. Layer that competitive fact onto the balance sheet: equity has been drawn down to just $48.8M against $2.14B of debt, funded by debt-financed buybacks, not organic FCF accumulation. A near-zero equity cushion means the company has almost no room to absorb a lost deal, an adverse IP ruling, or a partner-drug failure without a credit-quality scare. The 2029-to-2030 revenue dip already baked into FMP's own forward estimates ($2.01B to $1.78B) is the market's own model quietly agreeing that the patent-cliff risk is real, not a bear-side exaggeration.

Competitors: Alteogen (Korea, ALT-B4 hyaluronidase) is the direct head-to-head rival and has already won the highest-profile new mandate in the category (Merck/Keytruda SC) instead of Halozyme — a genuine market-share loss on the newest, largest decision point in the industry. Beyond Alteogen, large pharma partners increasingly have the option to develop in-house subcutaneous-conversion technology rather than license either party, which caps royalty economics industry-wide over time. On margins, Halozyme still leads today (77% gross / 57% operating margin, both expanding) versus Alteogen's much smaller, earlier-stage, and less profitable platform — Halozyme is larger and more proven, for now. Reinvestment runway favors Halozyme in the near term (established manufacturing relationships, an active BD pipeline evidenced by the new Incyte deal), but Alteogen's Merck win gives it a credibility flywheel of its own that could compound. Moat durability verdict: the switching-cost moat holds firmly for formulations ALREADY approved on ENHANZE, but does not extend automatically to new decisions — the moat is real but narrower than the 'once designed in, displacement is rare' framing implies, and Alteogen has proven it can win the biggest prize in the field.

#3ADBEAdobe Inc.BUY — Confirmed by financials:MEDIUM⭐ CIO BEST IDEA🥊 DEBATED🇺🇸 US⟳ ×7COREMoS +37%PEG 1.54▼

CIO take: 14x P/E for 37% ROIC and 89% gross margin is a trough multiple pricing in more AI-disruption fear than the 11%-growth reality currently supports.

Endorsed by: DeskContrarian, DeskScreener

🥊 Deep Research Memo (bull/bear debated)
Adobe is the dominant professional creative-software franchise (Photoshop, Premiere, Illustrator) plus Document Cloud and Experience Cloud, almost entirely subscription-recurring, printing an 89% gross margin and 37% operating margin on $23.77B FY2025 revenue (+11% YoY). Against named rivals — Figma (public, browser-native collaboration), Canva (private, ~$40B+, expanding into enterprise), and Salesforce (Experience Cloud rival) — Adobe still wins decisively on margin structure and enterprise entrenchment, but is losing share of new growth at the prosumer/SMB edge where those three compete hardest. Why now: the stock trades at a 14x trailing P/E, a historically depressed multiple for a company still compounding revenue at 11% with expanding buybacks (-4.7%/yr share count). That gap exists because the market is pricing meaningful AI-disruption risk into the multiple already — this is not a hidden risk the market has missed, it is a priced risk the market may be over-weighting relative to what the reported numbers currently show. Valuation and expected return: sell-side consensus target ($261.16) implies ~15% upside from $227.16; the screener's own DCF ($351.21, +35% MoS) should be treated as the optimistic case, not the base case, given how much more conservative the Street's own target is. Base-case expected return is ~12-15%/yr from buybacks plus high-single-digit organic growth plus a modest multiple recovery; bear case is roughly flat-to-negative if pricing power erodes faster than buybacks offset. The bear case — that generative AI collapses the need for Adobe's tools rather than just cheapening them, evidenced by the Morgan Stanley downgrade and a 46.6% institutional trim in this news window — is real and credible, but it has not yet shown up in the actual numbers: revenue has grown every year 2022-2025, margins are stable-to-improving, and Firefly gives Adobe its own generative offering rather than only a defensive posture. My honest rebuttal is that the current multiple already discounts a meaningful amount of this fear; the risk/reward favors owning it at 14x while watching closely, rather than avoiding it outright on a threat that hasn't yet dented the P&L. What to watch: Digital Media/Creative Cloud ARR growth rate and any explicit Firefly monetization disclosure in the next 1-2 quarterly prints, plus further sell-side rating changes. Exit trigger: two consecutive quarters of ARR growth decelerating meaningfully below the current ~11% trend, or a confirmed major enterprise defection to Figma/Canva/Salesforce, would flip this from BUY to AVOID — the thesis rests on the disruption fear being overstated, and a real deceleration would prove it isn't.

Business: Adobe sells the dominant professional creative/design software suite (Creative Cloud: Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere) plus Document Cloud (Acrobat/PDF) and Experience Cloud (enterprise marketing/analytics), almost entirely on recurring subscription revenue. FY2025 revenue was $23.77B, up 11% YoY, with 89% gross margin and 37% operating margin.

MOAT: WIDE — at least 2 independent sources (switching costs + brand/intangibles), backed by margin evidence moat — ['switching_costs: decades of embedded professional workflows (Photoshop/Premiere file formats, enterprise Experience Cloud integrations) make displacing Adobe costly for studios and marketing orgs', 'intangible_assets: Creative Cloud/Photoshop brand is effectively synonymous with professional creative work', 'pricing_power: 89% gross margin and 37% operating margin (FMP financial_statements) sustained across a decade of price increases']. Durability: . Key threat: Generative-AI content tools (Canva, Figma, in-model image/video generation) lower the skill floor for content creation, potentially commoditizing the individual-tool value proposition Adobe has priced on for 30 years — this is the single credible threat cited repeatedly in analyst downgrades (Morgan Stanley cut ADBE in the same news window this bundle covers).

Bull case: Own analysis: a genuine best-in-class software franchise trading at a historically depressed multiple (14x P/E) because the market is discounting AI-disruption risk more heavily than the actual reported numbers (11% revenue growth, stable margins) currently justify.

Bear case: Adobe's moat was built for a world where 'making' visual/video content required a skilled human operating a purpose-built tool. Generative AI collapses that premise: modern text-to-image/video models (and Adobe's own Firefly, tellingly built defensively rather than as an offensive new revenue engine) let a non-expert produce finished creative output with no Photoshop/Premiere workflow at all. That is a different, more dangerous threat than past 'cheaper alternative' competition (e.g. GIMP) because it doesn't just undercut price, it can remove the tool layer entirely for a growing share of use cases (social content, marketing assets, quick video edits). The market's own smart money is already voting: Morgan Stanley cut the stock in this exact news window, and an institutional holder (Andra AP fonden) trimmed 46.6% of its position. A 14x P/E is cheap only if 11% revenue growth persists — but growth compounding off subscription price increases (not net-new professional seats) is exactly the kind of growth that stalls fastest once a free/cheap AI-native substitute reaches 'good enough' for the median user. If Digital Media ARR growth slips toward mid-single digits over the next 2-3 quarters, the multiple does not have room to re-rate — it has room to fall further.

Competitors: Figma (now public post-2025 IPO) is the sharpest structural threat to Adobe's design tools: it is browser-native, real-time collaborative by design (Adobe retrofitted collaboration onto desktop-first tools), and it has a public war chest to keep undercutting Adobe on price for teams/agencies — the exact segment Adobe monetizes hardest. Canva (private, reported valuation well above $40B) has moved from consumer/SMB templates into enterprise brand-kit and video tools, directly encroaching on Creative Cloud's low-end and mid-market. Salesforce is the direct rival in Experience Cloud (enterprise marketing/analytics) — the bundle's own news flags this exact 'Salesforce vs Adobe: which enterprise software stock has the edge' debate live in the market right now. On margins: Adobe's 89% gross / 37% operating margin is still best-in-class and neither Figma nor Canva discloses comparable public profitability (Figma's post-IPO margins are still far thinner as it invests in growth) — so on pure margin structure Adobe still wins today. But reinvestment runway favors the challengers: Figma and Canva are growing their user base and product surface much faster off a smaller base, while Adobe's growth is increasingly price-increase-and-buyback-driven rather than seat-growth-driven. Verdict: the moat (switching costs + brand) still holds for entrenched enterprise workflows (video/print production pipelines, Experience Cloud integrations) but is genuinely eroding at the prosumer/SMB edge where Figma and Canva compete hardest — this is a moat under real pressure, not a moat that has already failed.

Capital allocation: B+

Valuation: P/E (TTM) 14.0, PEG 1.54 (forward-estimate basis) — cheap for a company compounding at 37% ROIC / 10.4% FCF yield. Sell-side consensus price target is $261.16 (vs. $227.16 spot, ~15% upside), materially below the screener's own DCF intrinsic value of $351.21 — that gap is the market pricing in real AI-disruption risk; treat the DCF number as the optimistic case, the $261 consensus target as the more grounded near-term marker.

Margin of safety: +35% below DCF ($351.21 DCF vs. $227.16 price), though only +15% below the more conservative sell-side consensus target of $261.16 — real but not as large as the DCF alone implies.

Expected return (3–5y): Base ~12-15%/yr (buybacks -4.7%/yr + high-single-digit organic growth + modest multiple re-rating from 14x toward high-teens as AI fears prove partly overblown). Bull ~20-25%/yr if the multiple re-rates to Adobe's historical 25x+ as the disruption narrative cools. Bear ~-5 to 0%/yr if Creative Cloud pricing power erodes faster than buybacks can offset. Key assumption: the 11% revenue growth rate holds and the multiple does not compress further from an already-depressed 14x.

What would change our mind: Two consecutive quarters of Digital Media (Creative Cloud) ARR growth below ~8% YoY; Firefly/generative credits failing to show up as a distinct, growing revenue line by FY2027; or a confirmed large-enterprise logo publicly switching its creative/marketing stack to Figma+Canva+Salesforce in combination.

Catalysts: Continued double-digit Creative Cloud/Firefly (Adobe's own generative AI) monetization; further buybacks (-4.7%/yr run-rate) mechanically lifting EPS; any stabilization in sell-side sentiment after the recent Morgan Stanley downgrade.

What to watch (4–12 wks): Next 1-2 quarterly prints for Creative Cloud/Digital Media ARR growth rate and any commentary on Firefly monetization; further sell-side rating changes in the 4-12 week window.

Time horizon: long

💼 Goldman Sachs Small-Cap — 5 picks ▼
💼 Goldman Sachs Small-Cap
Small-cap hidden-gem scanner: $100M-$2B cap, 25%+ growth, thin coverage, insider ownership, moat, catalysts, red flags.
📖 Strategy details▼

Goldman Sachs pre-discovery screen — finding companies growing 25%+ in the $100M–$2B range before mainstream institutional flows arrive. Goal: tomorrow's $10B company at $500M today.

  • Size: $100M–$2B market cap — big enough to be legitimate, small enough to still multiply
  • Coverage: 0–5 analysts covering the stock (≥20 = already discovered)
  • Revenue growth: minimum 25% YoY for 3+ consecutive quarters
  • Insider ownership: founders/executives holding 15%+ of shares (skin in the game)
  • Structural tailwinds: AI, cybersecurity, energy transition, aging demographics, automation
  • Unit economics: improving gross margins and positive operating leverage (revenue growing faster than costs)
  • Balance sheet: 18+ months cash runway without needing profitability
  • Blindspot channels: spinoffs from S&P 500 companies, foreign listings overlooked by US investors, orphaned small-caps that fell below $500M and lost analyst coverage, post-bankruptcy equities with clean balance sheets
  • Near-term catalysts: specific re-rating events within 6–12 months (earnings beats, product launches, regulatory approvals)

Peter Lynch's everyday-life observation framework. Simple, understandable consumer and workplace businesses growing 15–25%/yr at PEG <1.0. The best investments hide in plain sight — find them before Wall Street does.

💯 Mayer 100-Bagger — 3 picks ▼
💯 Mayer 100-Bagger
Small cap + high ROIC + owner-operator + long runway — the 100-bagger checklist. May return zero picks.
📖 Strategy details▼

Christopher Mayer's 100-Bagger framework — the research methodology identifying stocks with potential to return 100x, based on patterns observed across 365 historical 100-baggers.

  • Small starting cap: ideally under $1B — 100x must be mathematically possible
  • Long runway: serves a market large enough to support decades of revenue growth
  • ROIC above 20%: Mayer's single most predictive metric — the engine of compounding
  • Earnings growth: 20%+ annual earnings growth sustained for many years
  • Owner-operator: CEO and management with 10%+ personal stock ownership
  • Reinvestment runway: profits redeployed into new growth at high returns (not paid out as dividends)
  • No dilution: the company isn't issuing large amounts of new shares that erode long-term returns
  • Twin engines test: can earnings grow 10x AND the P/E multiple also expand to compound into 100x?
  • Time horizon reality: 100-baggers typically take 20–25 years — patience is the edge

🔢 Greenblatt Magic Formula — 10 picks ▼
🔢 Greenblatt Magic Formula
ROIC>20% + earnings yield>10% ranked screen, ex-financials/utilities/REITs. Top 10, not a curated shortlist.
📖 Strategy details▼

Joel Greenblatt's Magic Formula — the two-factor screen generating 30%+ annual returns over 20 years by finding companies that are simultaneously high-quality AND cheap.

  • ROIC above 20%: high-quality business generating strong returns on every dollar invested
  • Earnings yield above 10%: cheap relative to earnings (inverse of P/E) — the 'cheap' gate
  • Combined ranking: companies score best when BOTH metrics rank highly — quality + cheap together
  • Size filter: $50M–$10B to exclude illiquid micro-caps and already-covered mega-caps
  • Sector exclusions: skip financials, utilities, and REITs (different capital structures distort the formula)
  • Debt check: high ROIC shouldn't be mere financial leverage — verify balance sheet is clean
  • Earnings quality: free cash flow should match net income — flag accounting-driven earnings
  • Temporary vs permanent: is the stock cheap due to a fixable problem, or is the business structurally declining?

🎲 Pabrai Asymmetric Bet — 3 picks ▼
🎲 Pabrai Asymmetric Bet
3:1+ upside/downside bets with explicit downside protection — distress, special situations, hated industries.
📖 Strategy details▼

Mohnish Pabrai's Dhandho framework — combining LOW RISK (limited downside) with HIGH UNCERTAINTY (Wall Street can't value it) for asymmetric bets where heads I win big, tails I don't lose much.

  • Asymmetry ratio: upside potential ÷ downside risk must be 3:1 or better
  • Downside protection: what specifically limits the loss — asset value, cash, acquisition target, recurring revenue
  • Upside catalyst: the specific event that could drive 3–10x returns over 3–5 years
  • Temporary distress: markets treating a short-term problem (lawsuit, earnings miss, sector rotation) as permanent
  • Special situations: spinoffs, post-bankruptcy equities, rights offerings that create pricing inefficiencies
  • Hated industries: entire sectors abandoned by investors where survivors trade at distressed multiples
  • Margin of safety: gap between current price and conservative intrinsic value — the buffer against being wrong

🔄 Marks Second-Level — 5 picks ▼
🔄 Marks Second-Level
Consensus audit + second-level question — oversold/overbought extremes, narrative-vs-numbers gaps.
📖 Strategy details▼

Howard Marks' second-level thinking — first-level thinking gets average returns; second-level thinking ('the company is great BUT priced for perfection') finds the real opportunities.

  • Consensus audit: what is the mainstream view, and is it based on sound analysis or herd mentality?
  • Second-level question: what do I know or see that the consensus is missing?
  • Oversold opportunities: stocks down 50%+ where the negative narrative has become excessive vs fundamentals
  • Sentiment extremes: sectors at multi-year sentiment lows (rare to be wrong buying) or highs (rare to be right buying)
  • Narrative vs numbers gap: where does the market story ('this industry is dying') contradict the actual data?
  • Time horizon arbitrage: quarterly-focused Wall Street missing a multi-year thesis
  • Insider buying signal: executives aggressively buying when the market is selling — the strongest bullish insider indicator

🌀 Sleep Scale Economics Shared — 4 picks ▼
🌀 Sleep Scale Economics Shared
Businesses that share scale economics with customers via a reinforcing flywheel and long-term management.
📖 Strategy details▼

Nick Sleep's Scale Economics Shared framework — the methodology that identified Amazon, Costco, and Berkshire decades early, based on companies that share their scale advantages with customers to build a self-reinforcing flywheel.

  • Core test: does the company get MORE efficient and offer BETTER prices as it grows? (opposite of most businesses)
  • Customer obsession: willing to take short-term margin hits to give customers more value (Costco 15% margin discipline)
  • Flywheel: lower prices → more customers → more scale → lower costs → even lower prices (self-reinforcing loop)
  • Long-term thinking evidence: quarterly earnings suppressed for multi-year investment; founder letters emphasise decades
  • Customer lifetime value: expanding over time as the business creates more value per customer
  • Non-obvious moat: the advantage isn't patents or brand — it's a culture and business model the organisation embodies
  • Capital allocation: cash flow reinvested into high-return opportunities rather than buybacks at peak prices

🕳️ Burry Catalyst Deep Value — 4 picks ▼
🕳️ Burry Catalyst Deep Value
Hidden assets, sum-of-the-parts, activist/regulatory catalysts — each with an explicit timeline.
📖 Strategy details▼

Michael Burry's catalyst-driven deep value approach — finding mispriced assets where specific, identifiable catalysts will force the market to recognise hidden value within a defined timeframe.

  • Hidden assets: companies trading below the value of real estate, cash, or investments on the balance sheet
  • Sum-of-parts: conglomerates where individual divisions are worth more than the combined market cap

  • Accounting normalisation: one-time write-downs or unusual items temporarily depressing reported earnings
  • Catalyst timeline: each idea must have a specific catalyst with 6–18 month resolution — no 'cheap forever' open-ended theses

🛰️ Wall Street Blindspot — 5 picks ▼
🛰️ Wall Street Blindspot
Coverage-gap hunting — foreign listings, spinoffs, orphaned small-caps, sin-stock discounts — as a prioritized workflow.
📖 Strategy details▼

Wall Street Blindspot framework — finding investment opportunities that major banks structurally cannot or will not cover: coverage gaps, orphaned names, stigmatised sectors, complex structures.

  • Coverage gap: companies with 0–5 sell-side analysts — institutions only cover above $2B, leaving quality names persistently mispriced
  • Orphaned mid-caps: companies that fell below $500M and lost coverage — often trading at deep discounts to intrinsic value
  • Spinoff aftermath: newly independent companies facing forced selling from index funds in the first 18 months
  • Sin-sector discounts: quality companies in gambling, tobacco, fossil fuels, or defence at persistent ESG mandate discounts
  • Post-bankruptcy emergence: restructured balance sheets institutional investors can't own due to mandate restrictions
  • IPO aftermath: quality companies 18–24 months post-IPO when lockup expiry creates selling pressure
  • Key signal: the discount reason is structural or temporary, not fundamental — the business is better than the price suggests

💼 Goldman Sachs Small-Cap▼ full report
GOLDMAN SACHS SMALL-CAP HIDDEN GEM SCANNER — Desk Note, July 2026 1) ARTERIS, INC. (NASDAQ: AIP) Growth: FY2025 revenue $70.6M vs $57.7M in FY2024, +22.3% YoY, the fourth straight year of acceleration off a 2022 base of $50.4M. Coverage: thin — FMP forward-estimate panels show just 2 analysts modeling 2027 and 3 modeling 2028; this is a name institutional AI-semis desks have not fully onboarded. Insider Ownership: exceptional — founder/CEO K. Charles Janac directly and via Bayview Legacy LLC controls roughly 65% of shares outstanding (~30M of ~46M shares), a Nasdaq writeup flagged '44% ownership, insiders have a lot at stake' even before the fuller Janac stake became clear. Tailwinds: every AI accelerator and automotive SoC needs an on-chip interconnect (network-on-chip) to move data between cores — Arteris' FlexNoC/Ncore IP is licensed into designs at imec, SiEngine, and other AI/automotive silicon houses, a pure structural beneficiary of the custom-silicon boom. Unit Economics: ~90% gross margin (software/IP licensing model), the classic royalty-stream setup where each new design win is nearly pure incremental margin. Balance Sheet: $33.9M cash against only $9.1M debt — net cash despite the P&amp;L losses, giving genuine multi-year runway. Moat: patent-protected NoC IP plus multi-year chip design cycles create real switching costs once a customer taped out on Arteris IP. Catalysts: (1) royalty revenue scaling as licensed chips from FY23-24 design wins go into production, (2) further AI/HPC and automotive SoC licensing announcements, (3) a path to sustained profitability as fixed R&amp;D is spread over a larger royalty base. Red Flags: stockholders' equity is actually negative (-$14.6M in FY2025), and Janac has been running a steady 10b5-1 selling program through Bayview Legacy (multiple ~$1-2M weekly sales in June-July 2026) — pre-planned, but worth watching for pace. Verdict: the cleanest hidden-gem setup of the five — real AI-infrastructure moat, founder skin in the game far above screen, and a market cap (~$1.6-1.7B) still under the radar of most large-cap tech desks. 2) ONE STOP SYSTEMS, INC. (NASDAQ: OSS) Growth: 70.2% YoY revenue growth per recent filings — the strongest top-line number of the group, and management has described the quarter as a clear inflection point. Coverage: minimal; this is a sub-$200M name that only just qualified for Russell 2000 inclusion (effective June 29, 2026), which typically precedes, not follows, real sell-side pickup. Insider Ownership: not independently confirmed this cycle (web sources did not surface a current %), so this is the one pick where the ownership criterion is unverified rather than confirmed — treat as an open diligence item, not an assumption. Tailwinds: rugged, GPU-accelerated edge-AI compute and storage for defense, autonomous vehicles, and sensor-heavy industrial applications — a direct beneficiary of the push to run AI inference outside the data center. Unit Economics: gross margin surged to 58.5%, up sharply from prior periods, alongside the revenue acceleration — the improving-margin-plus-operating-leverage combination Goldman small-cap screens are built to find. Balance Sheet: market cap roughly $182M as of March 31, 2026, up 197% over the trailing year; specific cash/debt figures were not FMP-verified this cycle. Moat: reference-design relationships with GPU vendors and defense/industrial primes create integration switching costs, though the company competes against larger, better-capitalized system integrators. Catalysts: (1) Russell 2000 index-fund buying following the June 29 addition, (2) further edge-AI defense/industrial contract wins, (3) a maiden analyst initiation, which typically follows index inclusion for microcaps. Red Flags: this pick is entirely web-sourced — no FMP fetch was run, so treat headline growth/margin numbers as directionally right but not independently verified; small-cap liquidity and customer concentration risk are typical for a company this size. Verdict: the highest-momentum name on the list and worth a follow-up FMP pull before sizing, given it is the only pick here without a hard data check. 3) AMERICAN SUPERCONDUCTOR CORPORATION (NASDAQ: AMSC) Growth: FY2026 (ended March) revenue $299.2M vs $222.8M prior year, +34.3%, following +53% growth the year before — two consecutive years above the 25% bar. Coverage: essentially uncovered — FMP shows only 1 analyst modeling both FY2029 and FY2030. Insider Ownership: modest, not high — CEO Daniel McGahn (~1.18M shares) and CFO John Kosiba (~353K shares) together represent roughly 4-5% of the ~35M shares outstanding, well below the 15% target; this is a real gap versus the ideal screen. Tailwinds: AMSC sits at the intersection of two structural themes — AI data-center power bottlenecks driving grid-hardening demand, and offshore/onshore wind buildout — its CEO has explicitly framed the company around the 'AI energy bottleneck' in recent investor media. Unit Economics: gross margin expanded to ~29.8% from ~27.8% a year earlier as volume scaled through Grid and Wind segments. Balance Sheet: excellent — $144.2M cash against just $4.0M debt, net cash of $140.2M, comfortably 18+ months of runway even before the current profitability. Moat: patented high-temperature superconductor (HTS) wire and D-VAR reactive-power-compensation technology, plus multi-year utility qualification cycles that create real switching costs once installed. Catalysts: continued grid-hardening orders tied to AI/data-center power demand, wind-segment order flow, and potential re-rating if organic (non-M&amp;A) growth reaccelerates. Red Flags: independent analysis (Seeking Alpha, June 2026) flagged that headline growth is 'largely acquisition-driven' with organic Grid-segment growth in the high-single digits, and Wind-segment growth 'highly concentrated' in a single customer; separately, both the CEO and CFO sold stock in clustered transactions on June 8 and June 11, 2026. GAAP net income of $133.8M dwarfs EBITDA of $25.2M, implying a large non-operating/tax item inflating the bottom line — don't extrapolate that net-income number. Verdict: real thematic exposure and a fortress balance sheet, but the growth-quality and insider-ownership gaps mean this is a MEDIUM, not a top-conviction, idea until organic growth and insider buying (not selling) show up. 4) POWERFLEET, INC. (NASDAQ: AIOT) Growth: FY2026 (ended March) revenue $443.8M vs $362.5M FY2025, +22.4% — just under the 25% bar but the growth trajectory paired with a profitability inflection is the more interesting story. Coverage: 3 analysts modeling FY2028, 6 modeling FY2027 — slightly above the ideal 0-5 range but still a name most generalist funds haven't screened. Insider Ownership: reported inconsistently across trackers (roughly 6% per some sources, 22-23% per a more recent July 2026 pull) — flagging the discrepancy rather than picking the flattering number; needs a primary-source (proxy) check before relying on it. Balance Sheet: this is the weak link — $296.9M total debt against only $36.5M cash, net debt of $260.4M, inherited largely from the 2024 MiX Telematics combination. Moat: embedded hardware in customer vehicles plus an accumulating driver-risk dataset create real switching costs and a data network effect. Catalysts: (1) execution of the newly announced $30M buyback (signals management confidence despite leverage), (2) international SafeGuard rollout, (3) continued deleveraging from free cash flow. Red Flags: still GAAP-unprofitable (-$20.6M net loss) and the debt load is the single biggest swing factor for the thesis — this is a name where the balance sheet, not the growth story, will decide the outcome. Verdict: the operating-leverage inflection is real and underappreciated, but the debt load caps this at MEDIUM until net debt trends down. 5) EVOLV TECHNOLOGIES HOLDINGS, INC. (NASDAQ: EVLV) Growth: FY2025 revenue $145.9M vs $103.9M FY2024, +40.5%, following +29% growth the year before — the strongest, most sustained growth rate of the five, and a July 2026 Motley Fool headline cited a 45% jump in the most recent quarter. Coverage: sparse — 1 analyst modeling FY2028, 3 modeling FY2027. Unit Economics: gross margin ~51.6%; operating loss narrowed to -$44.8M from -$82.3M — meaningful operating leverage as the subscription base scales. Balance Sheet: $49.2M cash against $42.2M debt, roughly breakeven net cash — workable but not the fortress AMSC enjoys; burn rate needs watching against the August 11, 2026 Q2 print. Moat: a genuine AI data flywheel (more deployed scanners → more training data → better detection accuracy) plus high switching costs once a venue's security workflow is built around the platform. Catalysts: (1) Q2 earnings August 11, 2026, (2) further marquee-venue renewals/expansions, (3) potential resolution of the lingering governance overhang. Red Flags: a Seeking Alpha DCF piece (June 2026) pegged fair value at $6.59/share, well under trading levels, and flagged 'material internal control weakness' language still hanging over the stock — this is a name where the growth is real but the accounting/governance discount is earned, not paranoid. Verdict: best pure growth rate in the batch, but the insider-ownership gap and governance overhang keep this at MEDIUM rather than the top slot.
🛒 Lynch Buy What You Know▼ full report
BUY WHAT YOU KNOW — FIELD NOTES, SUMMER 2026 DUOLINGO (NASDAQ: DUOL) — [Fast Grower]. Here's the observation: I can't have a conversation with anyone under 30 without the green owl coming up — not the app, the owl, as a bit, a meme, a personality. That's the kind of ubiquity you used to only get from a Dunkin' Donuts on every corner. The company: Duolingo, obviously, no guessing required, no parent-company detective work. Category: Fast Grower — revenue growth has been running 35-38% and change, decelerating only slightly quarter over quarter, which is still plenty fast. Now the so-what test, the part everybody skips: is the stock priced like everybody already knows the story? A year ago it probably was — this thing traded at nosebleed multiples on hype alone. But after a hard pullback, the trailing P/E is sitting around 15x — cheaper than the average tech stock — for a business still growing better than 30%. That's the classic Lynch setup: a genuinely fast grower that the market temporarily decided to treat like a value stock. I'd rather buy the popular product after the crowd gets bored with the stock than while everyone's still bragging about it at the office. E.L.F. BEAUTY (NYSE: ELF) — [Fast Grower]. My teenage-niece test: what's in her makeup bag that costs less than a movie ticket. E.l.f. has been winning that fight for years, and now it owns Rhode too — the Hailey Bieber skincare line that's been driving the upside surprises in e.l.f.'s own guidance. Fiscal 2026 net sales grew 25% to $1.64 billion even while absorbing roughly 55% average tariffs, which tells you the pricing power and demand are real, not manufactured. Category: Fast Grower. So-what test: the stock is down 49% over the trailing year despite the sales growth holding up — that's a disconnect, not a red flag, assuming margins stabilize as tariff costs get absorbed or passed through. Analyst price targets averaging around $119 imply 50%+ upside from here. This is buy-what-you-know working the way it's supposed to: the product signal (viral TikTok launches, sold-out Rhode drops) showed up in the numbers before the stock caught up. CAVA GROUP (NYSE: CAVA) — [Fast Grower, priced for perfection]. The observation is dead simple: there's a Cava in every strip mall that used to have a Chipotle knockoff, and the line moves fast because people know exactly what they want. Same-restaurant sales are up 9.7% with real traffic growth (not just price hikes), revenue is up 32%, and management just raised the full-year same-store guidance. Great business. Now the so-what test, and this is where I have to be the bad guy: a 142x trailing P/E against an industry average forward multiple of 17x is not a valuation, it's a hope. Even with 20% unit growth for years to come, you are paying for a decade of flawless execution today. I like the burrito. I do not like the price of the stock that sells the burrito. File under: watch it, don't chase it, and remember that a popular product is not automatically a good stock. ON HOLDING (NYSE: ONON) — [Stalwart]. Every runner I know switched to On's Cloud shoes in the last two years, and it's not just runners anymore — the sneakers showed up on regular commuting feet, which is usually the signal a niche athletic brand has crossed into mainstream stalwart territory. Revenue grew 30% in 2025 and management is guiding to at least 23% growth for 2026 on a constant-currency basis. So-what test: forward P/E around 21x for 20%+ growth is not a bargain, but it's not the Cava problem either — one Simply Wall St narrative pegs fair value meaningfully above the current price. This is the un-sexy version of buy-what-you-know: no meme, no mania, just a shoe that keeps showing up on feet and a valuation that doesn't require perfection. POP MART / LABUBU (HKEX: 9992, OTC: POPCF) — [Fast Grower with real fad risk]. This is the single loudest 'what's suddenly everywhere' signal of the year — the fairy-tale plush monsters hanging off every other tote bag and backpack. 2025 sales surged 185% and profit 309%, almost entirely on the back of the Labubu-led Monsters line, which now accounts for roughly 40% of total revenue, up from 23% the year before. There is no clean U.S. pure play — Pop Mart trades in Hong Kong, thinly on U.S. OTC — so this is a fieldwork idea more than an easy portfolio addition. Category: Fast Grower, but I'd tag it with a giant asterisk for concentration/fad risk. The so-what test already happened in public: shares crashed over 22% in a single week in March 2026 the moment investors did the math on how dependent the whole company is on one character not going out of style. Management is guiding to 'no less than 20%' growth for 2026 — a deliberate pivot away from Labubu-fueled hypergrowth. This is exactly the stock Peter Lynch would tell you to research obsessively and then size very small: the observation is real, the company is real, but a one-character fashion cycle is a much shorter shelf life than a shoe or a makeup brand, and the stock already proved it will re-price violently on that fear.
📱 Camillo Social Arbitrage▼ full report
SOCIAL ARBITRAGE SCAN — PLATFORM SIGNALS BEFORE THE STREET QUANTIFIES THEM RHODE → E.L.F. BEAUTY (NYSE: ELF) Platform Signal: TikTok and Instagram, specifically Hailey Bieber's own channel plus the r/SkincareAddiction and beauty-TikTok ecosystem; Rhode product drops routinely sell out within hours and generate a wave of 'get ready with me' and restock-alert content. Velocity Metric (web-sourced, not FMP-verified): repeated 'sold out' restock cycles reported across 2026 launches, cited directly in e.l.f.'s own investor commentary as 'stronger-than-expected Rhode performance' driving a guidance raise — that's the rare case where the viral signal shows up in a public company's own words before the sell-side re-models it. Economic-Benefit Mapping: e.l.f. Beauty acquired Rhode in 2025; the parent company captures 100% of the economics, and fiscal 2026 net sales grew 25% to $1.64B partly on Rhode's contribution. This is about as clean a social-arb mapping as exists — the product going viral is unambiguously owned by a single, identifiable public equity. HOKA → DECKERS BRANDS (NYSE: DECK) Platform Signal: TikTok's run-club and 'ugly shoe' aesthetic communities, Strava activity-feed mentions, and Instagram marathon-culture content have carried HOKA from niche ultra-runner brand to mainstream must-have over the past 24 months. Velocity Metric: consistent multi-year double-digit brand growth reported within Deckers' portfolio (HOKA has been the standout growth engine relative to the more mature UGG brand), a pattern web-sourced from Deckers' own segment reporting rather than an independent tracker — flag as directional, not FMP-verified. Economic-Benefit Mapping: 100% of HOKA's economics flow to Deckers Brands, a large-cap with UGG as a second (more mature) leg — so the pure-play exposure is diluted relative to a single-brand company, but the mapping is direct and unambiguous. LABUBU → POP MART INTERNATIONAL GROUP (HKEX: 9992 / OTC: POPCF) Platform Signal: TikTok unboxing and blind-box-opening videos, Instagram tote-bag-charm culture, and a genuine secondary resale market (StockX-style flipping of rare Labubu variants) — arguably the single loudest cross-platform virality signal covered in this entire report. Velocity Metric: 2025 company-reported sales growth of 185% (to ~$5.4B) with the Labubu-led 'Monsters' line specifically growing to ~40% of total revenue from 23% the year before — a real, company-disclosed acceleration, though the forward-looking velocity (is it still accelerating in mid-2026?) is genuinely uncertain given the March 2026 stock crash on concentration fears. Economic-Benefit Mapping: Pop Mart captures the full economics as IP owner/manufacturer, but U.S. investors face real access friction — HK primary listing, thin U.S. OTC liquidity — which is itself part of why the signal may still be underexploited by U.S.-based social-arb capital even after the stock's run. WINGSTOP FLAVOR DROPS → WINGSTOP INC. (NASDAQ: WING) Platform Signal: TikTok and YouTube Shorts food-review content built around Wingstop's limited-time flavor launches and viral 'ranking every flavor' videos, a category of content that reliably spikes around new menu-item launches. Velocity Metric: same-store sales and digital-mix trends reported in Wingstop's own quarterly results have tracked closely with periods of heavier flavor-launch social content, though a hard, independently-verified correlation coefficient was not established here — this is a directional web-sourced observation, not a quantified backtest. Economic-Benefit Mapping: clean, single-brand pure play — all economics flow to Wingstop Inc. CELSIUS ENERGY DRINKS → CELSIUS HOLDINGS, INC. (NASDAQ: CELH) Platform Signal: gym-culture TikTok and Instagram content (aisle hauls, 'what I drink before leg day') drove Celsius from regional also-ran to top-three U.S. energy drink years ago. Velocity Metric: the signal that made Celsius a legendary social-arb case study (2021-2023) has since matured and decelerated as the brand became mainstream and shelf-space growth normalized — included here specifically as the cautionary counter-example: the platform signal that was once alpha is now common knowledge, and the Alani Nu acquisition adds real integration/execution risk rather than pure organic virality. Economic-Benefit Mapping: single-brand pure play, but conviction is LOW precisely because the edge has already been arbitraged away by the market.
💯 Mayer 100-Bagger▼ full report
MAYER100X -- Christopher Mayer 100-Bagger Framework Desk date: 2026-07-22 | Universe screened: local FMP cache (9,161 US-listed names, snapshot 2026-07-22T16:31 UTC) filtered for market cap approx &lt;$1.2B, ex-Financials/Utilities/REITs/Energy, ROIC(TTM) &gt;15%, and TTM revenue growth &gt;15%, cross-checked with WebSearch for ownership/qualitative facts. METHODOLOGY NOTE ON RIGOR Mayer's own 100 Baggers data shows the base rate for any single small-cap stock compounding 100x is extremely low even among "great business" candidates -- the framework is a filter for optionality, not a promise. I ran the full quantitative screen (market cap, ROIC, growth) against the cached FMP universe, then applied the qualitative criteria (owner-operator ownership, moat durability, dilution discipline, twin-engines) by hand against SEC/insider-ownership data pulled via WebSearch. Of roughly 20 quantitative survivors under $1.2B market cap, only three cleared enough of the seven criteria to be worth writing up as real candidates, and NONE cleanly passes the 10%+ founder-ownership bar -- which is itself the honest finding: true Mayer-style 100-baggers (small, high-ROIC, high-growth, AND heavily insider-owned, all four at once) are rare enough that a rigorous screen of the current US market turns up close to zero clean hits. I am presenting the three best partial matches with explicit pass/fail scoring rather than forcing a false positive. ------------------------------------------------------------- 1. CORMEDIX INC. (CRMD) -- $643M market cap (FMP, 2026-07-22) ------------------------------------------------------------- Business: Commercial-stage biopharma. Sole product DefenCath (taurolidine/heparin catheter lock solution) is the only FDA-approved therapy to reduce catheter-related bloodstream infections in adult hemodialysis patients via a central venous catheter. Approved Nov 2023, launched 2024, now scaling fast. Scoring grid (0-10, FMP TTM data + WebSearch, 2026-07-22): - Starting market cap &lt;$1B (ideally &lt;$1B, rarely works &gt;$5B): 9/10 -- $643M, squarely in the zone. - Long growth runway / large TAM: 7/10 -- current label is a single indication (hemodialysis catheter infection prevention), but management has guided a supplemental NDA filing 2H26 targeting the TPN (total parenteral nutrition) population, a market management itself sizes at $500-750M in incremental annual sales if approved (commercial launch targeted 2027, Phase 3 trending to completion 2028). Genuine large-market optionality, not yet in the base business. - ROIC &gt;15-20%: PASS, 10/10 -- FMP TTM returnOnInvestedCapitalTTM = 27.6%, now that the product has flipped from cash-burning to profitable. - 20%+ annual earnings growth potential: PASS, 10/10 -- TTM revenue growth of 617% (small-base launch-ramp effect) and FY26 consolidated revenue guidance raised to $325-345M (from a near-zero 2024 base); DefenCath-specific 2026 guidance $150-170M with a targeted TPN-driven step-up in 2027-28. - Owner-operator, 10%+ personal ownership: FAIL, 2/10 -- insider ownership is approximately 2.16% of shares outstanding per aggregated ownership trackers (institutional ownership ~21%, the rest public float). This is the single biggest crack in the thesis versus Mayer's own playbook (he specifically wants founders who eat their own cooking). - High-return reinvestment opportunity / durable moat: 7/10 -- moat is regulatory (FDA approval + first-mover exclusivity dynamics for the specific indication) plus no direct competitor in the category; durability depends on maintaining that exclusivity and successfully expanding into TPN before others try to enter. - Absence of heavy dilution: 6/10 -- share count grew during the pre-approval cash-burn years; now FCF positive (28% TTM FCF yield against a $643M cap) so forward dilution risk is much lower, but the balance sheet carries the scars of the pre-2024 dilutive era. Twin-engines test (can earnings 10x AND multiple expand?): Plausible on earnings (TPN approval alone could triple total DefenCath revenue by 2028); multiple expansion is less clear since the stock already re-rated hard off the FDA approval -- more of a "prove the TPN market" stock than a still-undiscovered one. Overall 100-bagger probability: LOW-to-MEDIUM (roughly 5-10%, generous by 100-bagger standards). The business quality and TAM optionality are real; the missing owner-operator alignment and already-partial re-rating are the drags. ------------------------------------------------------------- 2. ELECTROMED, INC. (ELMD) -- $336M market cap (FMP, 2026-07-22) ------------------------------------------------------------- Business: Designs and markets the SmartVest airway-clearance system for patients with chronic respiratory conditions (COPD, bronchiectasis, neuromuscular disease). Direct-to-patient and homecare-channel distribution model. Scoring grid: - Starting market cap &lt;$1B: 9/10 -- $336M, well within range. - Long growth runway / TAM: 5/10 -- respiratory airway-clearance devices are a real, growing niche (aging population, expanding bronchiectasis diagnosis rates) but not a sprawling addressable market on the scale of, say, a software platform; realistic ceiling is a multi-hundred-million-to-low-billions niche, not a market Electromed could 10x share of indefinitely. - ROIC &gt;15-20%: PASS, 7/10 -- FMP TTM ROIC 20.1%. - 20%+ growth potential: PARTIAL, 6/10 -- TTM revenue growth 17.0%, just under the 20% bar, though net income growth 46.3% shows real operating leverage. - Owner-operator 10%+ ownership: PARTIAL, 5/10 -- no single operating CEO owns 10%+; director/founder-adjacent Craig N. Hansen holds roughly 496,500 shares (~5.9% of the ~8.4M shares out), and Red Oak Partners (an activist/value investor, not an operator) holds the largest stake at 34.1%. Meaningful insider skin in the game exists but is not concentrated in the current CEO the way Mayer's framework wants. - Durable moat: 6/10 -- FDA-cleared device with established prescriber relationships and reimbursement codes creates real switching costs, but it is a narrower moat than a patented drug or network-effect software business. - Absence of heavy dilution: 8/10 -- small, disciplined share-count growth; company self-funds from FCF. Twin-engines test: Earnings 10x is a stretch given the niche-market ceiling described above; more realistic as a steady compounder than a 100-bagger. Multiple is already reasonable -- not deeply undiscovered, actively covered by small-cap value funds (Red Oak). Overall 100-bagger probability: LOW (roughly 3-5%). Good business, capped TAM. ------------------------------------------------------------- 3. CLIMB GLOBAL SOLUTIONS, INC. (CLMB) -- $480M market cap (FMP, 2026-07-22) ------------------------------------------------------------- Business: Value-added distributor connecting niche cybersecurity/infrastructure software vendors to a reseller network -- a "toll booth" model on emerging enterprise software categories, formerly Wayside Technology Group. Scoring grid: - Starting market cap &lt;$1B: 8/10 -- $480M. - Long growth runway / TAM: 6/10 -- distribution is inherently a lower-margin, market-share game rather than a proprietary-product moat with unlimited TAM; growth comes from picking winning vendor partnerships early, which is repeatable but not infinite. - ROIC &gt;15-20%: PASS, 6/10 -- FMP TTM ROIC 16.5%. - 20%+ growth potential: PASS, 9/10 -- TTM revenue growth 40.1%, one of the strongest growth rates in the small-cap-quality screen. - Owner-operator 10%+ ownership: FAIL, 4/10 -- CEO Dale Foster directly holds roughly 344,350 shares after 2026 grants against ~7M shares outstanding, approximately 4.9% -- real and growing (he has been a net accumulator via grants even while trimming via option-related sales), but below the 10% bar. - Durable moat: 5/10 -- vendor relationships and reseller-network lock-in provide some stickiness, but distribution moats are generally narrower than product moats and are exposed to vendor consolidation or disintermediation risk. - Absence of heavy dilution: 7/10 -- modest, compensation-related share growth only. Twin-engines test: Growth engine is genuinely strong (40%+ revenue growth); multiple-expansion engine is weaker since a distribution business rarely commands a re-rating to software-like multiples even if it keeps compounding. Overall 100-bagger probability: LOW (roughly 3-5%). Lesson for the framework: small-cap moat businesses with concentrated ownership are also the most likely to get bought out by a strategic before reaching 100x, which caps realized returns even when the underlying business thesis was correct. Consensus audit -- sound analysis, not pure herd mentality: FMP TTM data confirms real substance behind the fear. Second-level question: the bear case focuses on the capex outflow; the bull case (and the genuine second-level question) is whether the market is properly discounting the $553B contracted backlog and 84% cloud-infrastructure revenue growth reported in the Q3 FY26 print, i.e. whether today's negative FCF is "good" cash burn (pre-funding contracted future revenue at an attractive spread) rather than "bad" cash burn (spending into demand that may not materialize). The forward P/E of ~21 the market is assigning suggests investors are pricing SOME backlog conversion, but not full confidence in it. The real second-level edge here is in tracking quarterly backlog-to-revenue conversion and customer concentration (how much of that $553B rides on one or two AI customers) rather than simply "buying the dip" on headline oversold-ness -- this is a case for disciplined monitoring, not an immediate full-conviction buy. ------------------------------------------------------------- 2. NOMAD-STYLE NOTES: SCALE ECONOMICS SHARED, JULY 2026 The question I keep coming back to is not "how much does this business earn today" but "what does the business do with the extra dollar of scale, and who benefits." A company that becomes more efficient as it grows and then hands a meaningful share of that efficiency gain back to the customer, rather than to the income statement, is building a flywheel that competitors cannot easily copy -- because copying it requires giving up current profit for a long time, and very few managements (or their boards, or their shareholders) have the patience for that. That is the whole game: find the operators willing to look short-term "worse" so the business can be structurally better in ten years. Below are four businesses that, to varying degrees, exhibit that pattern today. 1) COSTCO WHOLESALE (COST) -- Conviction: MEDIUM Costco is the canonical scale-economics-shared business and the one I would point a student to first. The mechanism is almost embarrassingly simple: the membership fee is the profit engine, and the merchandise margin is capped, informally, at around 14-15% -- a self-imposed ceiling that management has talked about publicly for over two decades and has never really broken, even when Wall Street has begged them to. Every dollar of buying-power leverage that scale produces gets recycled into lower shelf prices, not fatter margins, which is why the count of paid members and the renewal rate (comfortably north of 90% globally) keep climbing. That is the flywheel: lower prices -&gt; more traffic and more members -&gt; more buying power and denser distribution -&gt; lower cost to serve -&gt; lower prices again. On the "suppressed near-term margins funding long-term reinvestment" test: Costco pays warehouse workers meaningfully above retail-sector norms, which shows up in the model as a near-term SG&amp;A drag relative to a peer that runs leaner staffing, but shows up in reality as far lower shrink, lower turnover, and a floor-level culture that becomes a genuine service moat competitors can't buy their way into within a single fiscal year. On founder/management signal: Jim Sinegal's original letters, and the culture he installed, are explicit that raising margin to "manage the number" is treated as a mistake, not a win, because it borrows against the membership relationship. Current management (Ron Vachris, following Craig Jelinek) has kept that religion -- no formal earnings guidance, share buybacks used opportunistically rather than to flatter EPS, and the membership fee itself raised only rarely and only after the value proposition has clearly widened further. On the numbers: FMP-verified financials (fetched directly, not estimated) show FY2025 revenue of $275.2bn, up from $254.5bn in FY2024 (+8.2%), net income up to $8.10bn from $7.37bn, and a net cash position of roughly $6.0bn (net debt of -$5.99bn) -- a balance sheet that is exactly what you'd expect from a management that treats capital conservatively and funds growth from its own flywheel rather than leverage. My hesitation, and the reason this is a MEDIUM rather than HIGH conviction pick today, is valuation: the market has fully priced this quality (consensus target north of $1,100/share on FMP data), so the business is excellent but the margin of safety is thin. Sleep-style investing does not require cheapness, but it does require patience with a full price, and I'd want a pullback before sizing this up. 2) MERCADOLIBRE (MELI) -- Conviction: HIGH MercadoLibre is running the Amazon-in-2005 playbook in a region with worse logistics infrastructure and higher fraud/credit risk, which is precisely why the moat, once built, is wider. As Mercado Envios (logistics) scales across Brazil, Mexico and Argentina, delivery times compress and cost per package falls, which lets the company both lower effective delivery costs to sellers (more sellers list, deeper selection) and extend free-shipping thresholds to buyers (more purchase frequency). The fintech arm, Mercado Pago, is the second leg of the flywheel: as transaction volume scales, MercadoLibre gets more repayment data per user, which lets it underwrite Mercado Credito loans to merchants and consumers who are functionally unbanked -- a customer-lifetime-value expansion that a pure marketplace could never capture. The near-term-margin suppression evidence is directly observable: MercadoLibre has spent over a decade running thin logistics and lending margins to build out fulfillment centers and a balance-sheet-funded credit book, in a region where most competitors gave up on logistics investment because it depressed near-term returns. Founder Marcos Galperin has run the company since 1999 and has been explicit, repeatedly, that near-term profitability is not the objective function -- share of wallet and repeat usage are. That is a long-term-thinking signal that has survived multiple currency crises and Amazon's on-and-off attempts to compete directly in the region. Not FMP-verified this round (no fetch run against MELI to conserve budget) -- this is training-knowledge-based, so treat the specific financial figures as approximate rather than sourced. 3) CHEWY (CHWY) -- Conviction: MEDIUM Chewy's flywheel is subscription-plus-service rather than pure price: Autoship locks in a recurring, predictable purchase, and the company has historically over-invested in customer service quality (hand-written notes, flowers sent to customers whose pets have died, a live customer-service culture that Amazon has never matched) at a cost that shows up as a margin drag versus a leaner competitor. As Chewy's regional fulfillment network and now Chewy Vet Care clinics scale, unit economics improve -- and management's public commentary continues to frame reinvestment into service and now healthcare verticals as the priority over near-term margin expansion, even as the business has begun to show that margin expansion is arriving anyway as a byproduct of scale, which is the tell you want: margin improves because scale created it, not because management decided to harvest. The customer-lifetime-value expansion case is straightforward -- Chewy is walking pet owners from a single commodity purchase (kibble) into pharmacy, insurance-adjacent products, and now veterinary care, extending the relationship across the entire pet lifecycle. That is a wallet-share flywheel, not just a scale flywheel, and it's the more interesting of the two for a long-duration holding. This is a lower-conviction, smaller-position idea than MercadoLibre because the moat (service culture) is real but more copyable over a long horizon than logistics infrastructure or embedded fintech data, and because post-founder-era continuity of culture is a genuine open question I would want to underwrite carefully before sizing up. Not FMP-verified. 4) RYANAIR HOLDINGS (RYAAY) -- Conviction: MEDIUM-HIGH Ryanair is scale economics shared applied to a commodity product (a seat) in an industry famous for destroying capital. The mechanism: as the airline scales its 737 order book and raises aircraft utilization, unit costs fall (fuel efficiency of newer airframes, better airport-slot economics, denser seating), and essentially all of that saved cost gets passed straight back into base fares that are frequently below cost, funded by ancillary revenue (bags, seat selection, priority boarding) -- a structure explicitly designed so the flywheel of "lowest fare in the market" keeps compounding share against flag carriers and other low-cost peers who cannot match the cost base. Founder/culture signal: Michael O'Leary is famously blunt about running the airline for decades at a cost obsession that borders on the theatrical, and -- more relevantly to the long-term-thinking test -- his personal compensation arrangements have historically been structured around multi-year share-price and profit thresholds that must be sustained, not simply touched once, which discourages the kind of short-term earnings management that a normal airline CFO might be tempted toward. The forward aircraft order book (locking in years of capacity growth at negotiated prices) is itself a long-duration reinvestment commitment that a management focused on next quarter's number would never sign. Not FMP-verified this round. I rate this MEDIUM-HIGH rather than HIGH only because airline economics remain exposed to fuel and macro shocks that can obscure the flywheel's progress for years at a time, and because -- with Brent trading near $94 amid Strait of Hormuz risk -- this is a genuinely bad month to be adding a fuel-sensitive flywheel story, even a structurally excellent one. I would want to see how the position performs through the current oil spike before increasing size. Portfolio-construction note in the Nomad tradition: I would rather own three or four of these at real size for a decade than own twenty at a fraction of a percent each. Scale-economics-shared businesses take years to prove out and are usually "too expensive" by conventional metrics the entire time -- that is the price of admission, not a reason to wait for a re-rating that may never come.

SCION-STYLE NOTES: CATALYST-SIZED DEEP VALUE, JULY 2026 I don't buy theses. I buy catalysts with a thesis attached. A cheap stock that stays cheap forever is not a trade, it's a tax write-off waiting to happen, so every name below is sized by how CERTAIN and how NEAR the catalyst is -- not by how much upside the sum-of-the-parts math implies. The math can imply 3x and I'll still underweight it if the catalyst is vague and the timeline is "eventually." Four names, ranked by catalyst certainty, highest first. 1) WARNER BROS DISCOVERY (WBD) -- 6-12mo catalyst -- Conviction: HIGH This is the highest-certainty situation on the list because the corporate action is already board-approved and in motion, not a thesis waiting for someone else to act on it. WBD committed to splitting into "Warner Bros." (streaming + studios: HBO Max, DC Studios, the film library) and "Discovery Global" (linear networks: CNN, TNT Sports, Discovery+, Bleacher Report), targeting completion around mid-2026. The board subsequently opened a formal strategic-alternatives review -- meaning the actual outcome could be the planned spin, an outright sale of the whole company, or separate transactions for each half -- but in every one of those branches, something happens to the stock within the next two to three quarters. That's the point: I am not betting on which path management takes, I'm betting that the multi-year era of "conglomerate discount because nobody can tell what this thing is worth" ends on a defined clock. Sum-of-the-parts logic here is straightforward -- a high-free-cash-flow, low-multiple linear-networks business bundled with a high-growth, high-multiple streaming and studio business has been systematically undervalued as a blend for years; separating them (or selling them to buyers who will pay up for the piece they actually want) is close to a mechanical re-rating. Certainty of SOME transaction: high. Certainty of exact terms/price: low -- which is exactly why this gets sized as my highest-conviction idea on the list, not because the thesis is the most dramatic (it isn't) but because the timeline is the least fake. 2) MOLINA HEALTHCARE (MOH) -- 6-18mo catalyst -- Conviction: MEDIUM-HIGH This is an accounting-normalization trade on a business I actually hold. Molina's medical-loss ratio has been running hot -- full-year 2026 Medicaid MLR guidance sits at 92.9%, and management itself has called 2026 "a trough year for Medicaid industry margins" because state rate-setting has lagged actual medical-cost trend. That is a real, admitted mismatch, not a permanent structural impairment: state Medicaid rates get reset (and sometimes trued-up retroactively, as happened in 2025) on a predictable actuarial cycle, and Molina's own Q1 2026 print came in better than guided (91.1% consolidated MLR) with management flagging optimism about further off-cycle rate adjustments. The company has reaffirmed full-year guidance of at least $5 in adjusted EPS on roughly $42bn of premium revenue despite the noise. This is the classic Burry setup: a one-time (or few-year) cost/rate mismatch is being read by the market as a permanent margin reset, when the actual mechanism -- state rate-setting catching up to trend -- runs on a known calendar. Certainty is medium-high because the rate-reset mechanism is procedural and recurring, not speculative; the open question is only how many quarters of pain come before the trueup, which is why the catalyst window is wide (6-18 months) rather than a single date. 3) BRUKER CORPORATION (BRKR) -- 1-2yr catalyst -- Conviction: MEDIUM Another name I actually hold, and a cleaner cyclical-trough story than a permanent-impairment one. Bruker's scientific-instruments business has been hit by the collapse in U.S. academic and government life-sciences capex tied to NIH funding uncertainty -- the company is planning around potential NIH budget cuts of up to 20% for FY26 -- which has pushed organic revenue growth negative (down 4.4% in Q1 2026) even as reported revenue ticked up 2.7% on FX and bolt-on contribution. But the order book tells a different story than the reported top line: Scientific Instruments bookings grew high-single-digits organically in Q1, academic orders ex-US grew double digits, and molecular-diagnostics placements ran 40% ahead of internal plan -- those reagent-rental placements are booked as capex today and convert into a recurring consumables annuity over the following several years. This is a business where the reported numbers look worse than the underlying demand signal because a policy-driven funding air-pocket (NIH budget uncertainty) is depressing the segment that gets the headline attention, while the higher-quality recurring-revenue engine underneath keeps compounding. Certainty is only medium because the NIH funding catalyst genuinely depends on U.S. political outcomes I can't underwrite with precision, and the timeline (1-2 years for a funding-environment normalization) is soft. 4) MACY'S (M) -- 1-3yr catalyst, LOWEST certainty -- Conviction: LOW-MEDIUM (position sized small) This is the textbook hidden-real-estate-asset thesis, and it is the one on this list I trust the LEAST, precisely because the catalyst has already failed once and has no live process today. Arkhouse and Brigade walked away from their buyout approach (ultimately rejected by the board in July 2024 after multiple bid increases, topping out around $6.9bn / $24.80 per share) on grounds the board called insufficiently financed -- and as of today there is no active takeover process, just a activist sponsor who has said the door "isn't closed" and a company-run program to shutter roughly 150 underproductive stores by 2026, which is itself a slow-motion way of monetizing real estate without a third party forcing the issue. The real-estate NAV argument (flagship locations like Herald Square carrying material land value the market cap doesn't reflect once you strip out the operating retail business) is sound arithmetic, but arithmetic is not a catalyst. I am carrying this at low-medium conviction and a correspondingly small position specifically to make the point that thesis quality and catalyst certainty are different axes -- Macy's real-estate math may be just as compelling as WBD's sum-of-the-parts math, but WBD has a board resolution and a clock, and Macy's has a rejected bid and a hope that someone tries again. Sizing discipline: WBD &gt; MOH &gt; BRKR &gt; M, in that order, strictly because that is the order of catalyst certainty, not thesis elegance. If a new activist re-emerges at Macy's with financing in hand, this ranking changes immediately -- until then, it stays the smallest position.

WALL STREET BLINDSPOT — PRIORITIZED HUNTING WORKFLOW, JULY 2026 STEP 1 — START WITH THE ZERO-COVERAGE SCREEN, BECAUSE IT'S THE CHEAPEST TO RUN AND THE HIGHEST SIGNAL-TO-NOISE. Before hunting anything exotic, run a straight 'no news, no analysts' filter across small-caps you already have data access to. That's exactly how CoreCard Corporation (NASDAQ: CCRD) surfaced this cycle: an FMP data pull returned a literal 'no news available' error for company news, and only a single analyst forward estimate exists in the system. CoreCard is not obscure by accident — it was spun off from Intelligent Systems Corporation, founder J. Leland Strange still holds a massive personal stake (over 1.3M shares moved in a single 2025 disposition event alone), and the company quietly produces card-processing software with real margins (2024 revenue $57.4M, EBITDA $10.1M, net cash position). This is the single highest-priority category precisely because a zero-coverage screen costs nothing to run and immediately tells you where the herd literally cannot be looking. Action: pull full financials, verify the spin-off cap structure, and size a starter position before the first sell-side initiation changes the picture. STEP 2 — NEXT, MINE THE 'ORPHANED FORMER MID-CAP' BUCKET, BECAUSE THE FUNDAMENTALS ARE ALREADY PROVEN. Once the true zero-coverage names are exhausted, move to companies that used to have real institutional attention and lost it as market cap drifted below the $500M-$1B threshold that keeps most funds interested. Preformed Line Products Company (NASDAQ: PLPC) fits perfectly: only 1 analyst is modeling out to 2029 in FMP's system, the insider trading log is dominated by a tight cluster of family-adjacent names (Klaus, Ruhlman, Hofstetter, Morcos) executing routine equity-plan dispositions rather than institutional-scale trading, and the company just got a rare bit of press — Zacks flagged it in May 2026 as one of '2 Small Cap Power Plays With Data Center Optionality.' Revenue is $669M, dividend-paying, net cash positive. This is a name Wall Street used to know and forgot; the data-center power-infrastructure narrative gives it a fresh, underpriced catalyst. Action: confirm the family/insider ownership concentration via the proxy, then treat any coverage initiation as the exit signal, not the entry signal. STEP 3 — THEN WORK THE FOREIGN-LISTING BLINDSPOT, WHERE THE DISCOUNT IS STRUCTURAL, NOT FUNDAMENTAL. U.S. investors systematically underweight anything not on the NYSE or Nasdaq main board. Kambi Group plc (Nasdaq First North Growth Market: KAMBI) is the textbook case: a genuinely mission-critical B2B sports-betting technology supplier (odds compiling, risk management, front-end UX for licensed operators across the Americas, Europe, and Australia) trading at a $352M market cap on a Swedish growth-market exchange most U.S. terminals don't even default-populate. It carries a double discount — foreign-exchange obscurity stacked on gambling-adjacent sin-stock avoidance — for a company whose revenue (~$181M trailing) is generated mostly from U.S. operator relationships. Action: verify ADR/OTC accessibility and settlement mechanics before sizing; this category requires the most operational diligence of the five. STEP 4 — LAYER IN THE SIN-STOCK DISCOUNT, WHICH COMPOUNDS WELL WITH COMPLEX HOLDCO STRUCTURES. Vector Group Ltd. (NYSE: VGR) sits at the intersection of two blindspot categories simultaneously: it's a discount-cigarette manufacturer (Liggett Group, Vector Tobacco) bolted onto a New York real estate arm (New Valley LLC), a structure complex enough that generalist funds often pass rather than build a sum-of-the-parts model, and it's excluded outright from most ESG-mandated portfolios as a tobacco name. The result is a forward dividend yield north of 5.3% that would look expensive to replicate anywhere else in consumer staples. Action: build the sum-of-the-parts (tobacco cash flow plus real estate NAV) that most ESG-constrained funds never bother to construct. STEP 5 — LAST, MONITOR THE FRESH-SPINOFF CALENDAR, BUT DON'T ACT UNTIL THE TICKER AND INDEX MEMBERSHIP SETTLE. Mobility Global, S&amp;P Global's mobility-data-and-analytics spinoff, distributed to shareholders effective July 1, 2026 (alongside Middleby's Midera spinoff on July 6), represents the freshest and highest-risk category: day-one-to-week-two post-spinoff, when index funds tracking the parent are still mechanically dumping shares of the new entity regardless of fundamentals, and no analyst model exists yet. This is deliberately ranked last and LOW conviction — the ticker and regular-way trading were still stabilizing as of this report, so there's no verifiable financial data to underwrite a real position yet. Action: watch for the forced-selling window (typically 4-8 weeks post-distribution) and revisit with real financials once the entity has reported at least one standalone quarter — acting before then is speculation, not analysis.
